Gastrointestinal Disorders

Bowel Obstruction

Bowel obstruction is an ED resuscitation, imaging, and consultation problem: determine whether symptoms represent ileus, partial/complete mechanical obstruction, closed-loop obstruction, ischemia, perforation, or pseudo-obstruction.

Board trap: Do not dismiss obstruction as constipation when pain, vomiting, distention, obstipation, leukocytosis, peritonitis, or CT transition point is present.

BOWEL OBSTRUCTION

INTRODUCTION

Intestinal obstruction prevents regular passage of food and bowel contents. Mechanical obstruction results from intrinsic, extrinsic, or intraluminal factors, while adynamic ileus is impaired motility and usually self-limited. Differentiating small from large bowel obstruction affects likely cause, imaging interpretation, and surgical urgency.

PATHOPHYSIOLOGY

Obstruction traps gas and secretions, worsened by vomiting and decreased intake, leading to volume depletion, electrolyte abnormalities, hemoconcentration, renal injury, and shock. Distention raises intraluminal pressure, reduces venous/lymphatic drainage, and can progress to ischemia. Closed-loop obstruction can deteriorate rapidly because both ends are occluded and contents cannot decompress.

SMALL BOWEL OBSTRUCTION

SBO accounts for most bowel obstructions. Adhesions after surgery are the most common cause; hernias, internal hernias after Roux-en-Y bypass, tumors, inflammatory bowel disease, intussusception, bezoars, gallstone ileus, parasites, radiation injury, duodenal hematoma, and capsule retention are important alternatives. Prior abdominal surgery does not exclude hernia, cancer, or ischemic complications.

LARGE BOWEL OBSTRUCTION

Large bowel obstruction is most often due to neoplasm, particularly in older patients. Diverticulitis, fecal impaction, sigmoid volvulus, cecal volvulus, strictures, and pseudo-obstruction are additional causes. LBO more commonly produces prominent distention and hypogastric pain, and cecal or closed-loop physiology can threaten perforation.

CLINICAL FEATURES

HISTORY

Pain is usually crampy and intermittent in mechanical obstruction; vomiting pattern suggests level. Proximal SBO often causes bilious vomiting, distal SBO may produce feculent vomiting, and LBO tends toward hypogastric pain, constipation, and distention. Prior surgeries, hernias, malignancy, inflammatory bowel disease, radiation, bariatric procedures, opioids, and anticholinergics matter.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION

Distention is often the most reliable sign of SBO. Bowel sounds may be high-pitched early and absent late. Localized tenderness, rebound, fever, tachycardia, hypotension, or toxic appearance should be treated as possible strangulation or perforation until proven otherwise. Hernia exam, rectal exam, stool/blood assessment, and pelvic exam in selected patients help avoid missed extrinsic or alternative causes.

DIAGNOSIS

Consider obstruction or ileus in abdominal pain with distention, vomiting, constipation/obstipation, or high-risk history. Many pathology processes can mimic the presentation, so diagnosis requires exam plus imaging and labs rather than symptoms alone.

LABORATORY TESTING

CBC, electrolytes, renal function, lactate/acid-base assessment when sick, and targeted labs help estimate dehydration and ischemia. Leukocytosis, left shift, or extreme counts increase concern for gangrene, abscess, peritonitis, or mesenteric vascular occlusion. Normal labs do not rule out obstruction or early ischemia.

IMAGING

Plain abdominal films have limited utility and can mislead when stool burden is present. CT abdomen/pelvis is the imaging method of choice because it detects obstruction, transition point, cause, closed-loop configuration, ischemia, perforation, abscess, tumor, and alternative diagnoses. Oral contrast is not always necessary and can delay imaging.

TREATMENT AND DISPOSITION

Initial care is NPO, IV access, isotonic fluids, electrolyte correction, antiemetics, analgesia, and NG decompression for significant vomiting, distention, or high-grade obstruction. Treat sepsis and suspected ischemia early. Admit patients with bowel obstruction; surgical consultation is required, urgently when peritonitis, strangulation, ischemia, perforation, closed-loop obstruction, complete obstruction, or systemic toxicity is possible.

Adynamic ileus or uncertain low-risk presentations may receive conservative care with observation, hydration, medication review, and correction of metabolic triggers. Mechanical obstruction requires serial exams and definitive inpatient management. Disposition is not complete until the patient has a monitored pathway and a responsible surgical/medical team.
